# Moelis & Company (MC) — Forensic Dossier

*Six consecutive earnings calls: Q1-2025 (2025-04-23) → Q1-2026 (2026-04-29). Pure-play independent M&A / restructuring / capital-markets advisory boutique. Founder-CEO transition mid-stream (Ken Moelis → Navid Mahmoodzadegan, Q2-2025).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The arc across these six quarters is a **textbook advisory-boutique cyclical round-trip dressed as a secular growth story** — and the dress is starting to slip in the final quarter.

- **Q1-2025 (Ken Moelis):** Story opens on a high — "record new business origination and a record pipeline," "very bullish point of view for 2025." Then "Liberation Day" (April 2 tariff shock) hits between the quarter-end and the call. Backlog admitted down from $331M; Ken frames it as "temporary," "in the control of the administration," explicitly contrasting it with COVID/GFC ("outside the control"). Core thesis already in place: the **four growth pillars** — M&A, capital markets, restructuring/CSA, and the new **Private Capital Advisory (PCA / GP-led secondaries)** build-out.

- **Q2-2025:** Whiplash recovery. Revenue $365M (+38%), "highest second-quarter revenues on record." "We're kind of back as of now very close to the level of enthusiasm that was prior to April 2." Two structural reveals: (1) the **CEO transition** — Ken to Executive Chairman, Navid to CEO; (2) the **excess-capital admission** — "we probably have more excess capital than we want or need… stock repurchase will probably play more prominently." This is the first capital-return signal and the seed of the eventual buyback.

- **Q3-2025 (Navid's first call):** Peak-confidence quarter. $376M (+34%), 9-month revenue +37%, "pipeline remains near all-time highs." Name-drops trophy mandates (Essential Utilities, the Delaware AG on OpenAI's recap, NY Giants minority stake). Frames the cycle as "a steadily improving **multiyear** M&A cycle" — the language shifts from cyclical-recovery to secular-runway. Capital markets "more than double" prior-year; PCA "fourth pillar." First buyback execution (206k shares, $14.5M). **CSA/restructuring quietly flagged DOWN** ("less new origination than a year ago").

- **Q4/FY-2025 (2026-02-04):** The victory lap. Record Q4 $488M, FY revenue $1.54B (+28%), adjusted EPS $2.99 (+64%), comp ratio crushed to 65.8% (−320bp), pretax margin 21.5% (+510bp). Big capital-return pivot: $284M returned in 2025, **new $300M open-ended buyback authorized**, 716k shares bought in Q4 at $62.96. Trophy mandate list expands (Netflix/WBD, Allied Gold/Zijin, Ventyx/Lilly, USA Rare Earths/DoC). Navid's three pillars: "clients, culture, growth."

- **Q1-2026 (2026-04-29) — THE TURN:** Revenue **$320M, +4% YoY** — a violent deceleration from +34/38/41% prints. Pretax margin back down to **15%** (from 28.6% in Q4). Comp ratio back to 65.8% but non-comp ratio spikes to 21%. EPS **missed** ($0.50 vs $0.56 est). Now the headwinds are explicitly named: "**war in the Middle East, disruptions in private credit, and the impact of AI on certain sectors**." CSA pipeline "meaningfully above last year" but capital-markets and CSA revenue *declined* in the quarter. PCA still "ramping" — "not going to see a lot of actual revenues… in 2025." The "multiyear cycle" language survives but is now hedged with "we'll see how the year plays out."

**Drivers introduced:** PCA / GP-led secondaries (the genuine new growth leg, but still pre-revenue); AI as a productivity lever *and* a restructuring tailwind. **Drivers quietly contracting:** restructuring/CSA (record 2024 → down 2025); the cyclical M&A tailwind that did all the FY-2025 heavy lifting visibly stalled in Q1-2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

On those, they delivered: the "temporary" April-2 shock did prove temporary; the pipeline-to-revenue conversion showed up in the record fourth quarter; the comp-ratio improvement they hinted at materialized (65.8%). The screener's **beat rate of roughly 86% (6 of 7 quarters)** corroborates a reliable-execution reputation — but note that streak **broke in the first quarter of 2026** with an ~11% miss. Reliability: **Medium-High, with a fresh crack.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Comp ratio flexibility** — asked every quarter. Management repeatedly deflected to "it's all top-line driven," refusing a formula. This is the analysts' central worry: in a downturn, comp is sticky (you must pay bankers to retain them), so margins compress fast when revenue falls. The first quarter of 2026 is the test case, and early evidence (EPS −25%) suggests the fear is warranted.
- **Excess capital return** — analysts pushed on the $849M cash pile; management conceded "we probably have more capital than we need" and leaned into buybacks. This has now begun in size (see below).
- **Restructuring counter-cyclicality** — analysts probed whether the restructuring desk would cushion a slowdown; management admitted restructuring was *declining* because financing markets were too easy, removing the natural hedge.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Genuine operating leverage and a fortress balance sheet (no debt, large cash).
🟢 Top-of-group revenue growth and returns (ROE ~35%, ROIC ~22%) when the cycle cooperates.
🟢 Credible, well-integrated growth investment in Private Capital Advisory (secondaries), a real secular-growth adjacency.
🔴 **Extreme cyclicality** — a GAAP loss as recently as 2023; five-year EPS growth is negative; 2021 remains the unbeaten peak.
🔴 **The freshest data point is a miss** — Q1 2026 EPS −25% YoY, an ~11% consensus miss, stock down ~6%. The "multiyear up-cycle" thesis is being tested in real time.
🔴 **Valuation offers no margin of safety** — the screener's own blended fair value (~$44.5) sits ~35% *below* the ~$68.5 price. The "deep value" label is not supported by the numbers.
🔴 Removal of the comp-ratio formula reduces expense accountability heading into a potential slowdown.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"Deep value" is a misread.** The signal that flagged this name treats a ~10x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple as cheap, but that multiple sits on **peak-of-recovery** free cash flow. Advisory boutiques always look cheap on trailing earnings at the top of a fee cycle and expensive at the bottom — the multiple is a cyclical trap, not a value signal. The blended fair value below the price confirms it.
- **The buyback is the real capital-allocation shift.** Management pivoted from hoarding cash to returning it: a new $300M authorization, ~950k shares repurchased in 2025, and **~1.9M shares bought in the first quarter of 2026 at ~$61.40** (per the Q1 2026 release), drawing cash down to ~$354M. This is a genuine, dated support under the stock — but it is a valuation cushion, not a re-rating catalyst.
- **Restructuring hedge quietly gone.** The one business that normally protects advisory firms in a downturn (restructuring) has been de-emphasized because easy credit killed the demand — which means a real slowdown would hit revenue with less internal offset than usual.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE** (a well-run, well-capitalized franchise in a genuine but maturing recovery, now showing its first negative quarter).

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a high-quality but deeply cyclical advisory fee stream priced with no margin of safety, and the most recent quarter went backwards.** The bull case ("multiyear up-cycle") and the bear case ("2021 was the peak; the cycle is rolling over") are both live, and the freshest evidence tilts toward the bear.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat is an intangible-brand / relationship-and-talent moat — Ken Moelis's franchise, senior-banker relationships, and culture. It is real (returns on capital in the low-20s% prove pricing power in good years) but it is **not a switching-cost or network moat**; the assets walk out the door every night, and roughly a third of managing directors have under three years on the platform, so the earnings base is talent-dependent and not contractually locked. **Moat trend: STABLE** — the returns are high but violently cyclical, not durably rising.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** There is no terminal-value story here. If anything, AI-driven corporate disruption is a *tailwind* for M&A and restructuring demand (management explicitly frames it that way). The risk is cyclical, not structural.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Moelis & Company is a genuinely improving franchise that has just been handed the best dealmaking backdrop in five years, and that the 2025 operating leverage is the start of a trend rather than a one-off. The evidence for the improvement is unusually clean. Full-year 2025 adjusted revenue grew 28% to $1.54 billion; the compensation ratio -- the share of revenue paid out to bankers, which is the single number that decides profitability at an advisory firm -- fell 320 basis points to 65.8%; the non-compensation ratio fell from 15.9% to 14.6%; and adjusted pre-tax margin expanded 510 basis points to 21.5%. Adjusted earnings per share rose 64%, from $1.82 to $2.99. Management then guided 2026 compensation to 'a similar comp ratio to where we ended the year at, that 65.8%' (4 February 2026 call) and hit exactly 65.8% in the first quarter -- a firm that guides its most important cost line to the decimal and lands it is not a firm losing control of its own economics.

The second leg is that the earnings base is still ramping. On the 4 February 2026 call the chief executive disclosed that 'about 1/3 of our MDs have been MDs on the platform for less than 3 years, and about 1/4 of our MDs have been MDs on the platform for less than 2 years.' An advisory managing director typically takes two to four years to reach full productivity, so a third of the senior roster is not yet earning what it will earn. Headcount went from 170 managing directors in September 2025 to 178 by February 2026, with eight more hired year-to-date in 2026. If the cohort matures at anything like historical rates, revenue per banker rises without a proportional cost increase, and the compensation ratio has room to fall further -- the chief financial officer confirmed in April 2026 that 'if the environment improves and we ultimately have revenues of what we would expect, we will have an improvement in comp ratio.'

The third leg is the new fourth business line. Private capital advisory -- advising private-equity sponsors on continuation vehicles and secondary sales of fund stakes -- went from one senior hire in early 2025 to seven dedicated managing directors by early 2026, into a market management describes as hitting 'record levels.' Crucially, this is the fastest-ramping form of advisory hire, because the clients already exist: 'we're just plugging a product set into an existing set of relationships, and it's working really beautifully' (February 2026). This line contributed almost nothing to 2025 revenue by management's own admission, so anything it earns in 2026 and 2027 is incremental.

The fourth leg is the macro tape. Global merger activity set an all-time first-half record in 2026 at roughly $2.8 trillion announced, up 48% year over year, with megadeals close to half of value and antitrust review unusually permissive. Moelis has been visibly on the marquee mandates -- Netflix/Warner Bros., Clear Channel Outdoor's $6.2 billion sale, Kennedy Wilson's $9.5 billion take-private, TriPointe Homes' $4.5 billion sale, the Delaware Attorney General on OpenAI's recapitalisation, X-energy's $1.2 billion initial public offering. Management has also been consistently right about this cycle before: they called the April 2025 tariff shock temporary while it was happening, and revenue grew 38% the following quarter.

The fifth leg is capital discipline. Zero borrowed money; roughly 950,000 shares repurchased in 2025 and another 1.9 million in the first quarter of 2026 (895,000 of them in the open market at an average of $61.40); a new $300 million authorisation in February 2026; and a $0.65 quarterly dividend held through the entire cycle. Management flagged excess capital in July 2025 and acted on it within one quarter.

What must hold for the bull case: the middle market has to actually open -- management has now promised this twice, in October 2025 and again in April 2026. Revenue has to reaccelerate from the first quarter's 4% toward the 11% implied by the $1.71 billion 2026 consensus. The private-credit disruption that management named as a first-quarter-2026 headwind has to stay contained rather than freezing sponsor financing. And the compensation ratio has to hold at or below 65.8% while eight new managing directors are absorbed. If all four hold, 2027 consensus earnings of $3.92 per share are achievable, and a high-quality advisory franchise growing into a multi-year cycle would not obviously be capped at today's multiple.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the business to be bad. It requires only that the price already contains everything the bull case is waiting for -- and on live market data, it does, twice over.

Start with the deceleration, because it is the newest fact. Year-over-year revenue growth ran +41%, +38%, +34%, +11% and then +4% in the first quarter of 2026. Quarterly earnings per share fell 25% year over year. The company missed consensus at $0.50 against $0.59 -- a 15% shortfall and the first miss in seven quarters. Management's own framing changed with it: the April 2026 call opened by naming 'the war in the Middle East, disruptions in private credit and the impact of AI on certain sectors' as headwinds, and conceded 'we have to transact against that pipeline, and some of that is out of our control.' A year earlier the constraint was described as temporary and externally imposed; now it is described as beyond the firm's control.

Second, the pipeline claim has stopped carrying information. 'Pipeline near record levels' or 'near all-time highs' has been asserted in four consecutive calls -- July 2025, October 2025, February 2026 and April 2026 -- across a four-fold collapse in the rate at which that pipeline converts into revenue. A claim that is true in every state of the world tells an investor nothing. The same applies to the middle-market promise, made in October 2025 ('we think that's coming') and re-made verbatim in April 2026 ('it will just take time for that middle market to open up, but it's coming'). That forecast has been re-dated, not delivered.

Third, and decisively, the valuation. At $68.18 the shares trade at roughly 24.5 times trailing twelve-month diluted earnings of $2.78, about 22 times the 2026 consensus of $3.09, roughly 17 to 18 times enterprise value to trailing earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, and about 3.6 times enterprise value to revenue. Measured live on 27 July 2026, every one of those is the highest in the peer group: Evercore trades at 17.5 times trailing earnings and 12.4 times enterprise value to that cash-earnings measure, PJT Partners at 20.1 and 11.0, Houlihan Lokey at 22.2 and 13.9, Lazard at 18.8 and 13.2. Moelis is not the cheap boutique -- it is the expensive one, and it is the one that just missed.

Fourth, the screen that surfaced this name as deep value is measuring an accounting artifact. The 99.2% gross margin and 9.8 times price to free cash flow that flagged it do not survive inspection: three of the last four quarters classify roughly two-thirds of revenue as cost of revenue (bank compensation), while the fourth quarter of 2025 classifies almost none, inflating trailing gross profit by close to $295 million. Restating that quarter consistently at the disclosed 61.1% compensation ratio, trailing gross profit is roughly $514 million rather than $809 million, and enterprise value to gross profit is about 10.8 times -- against roughly 5.3 times at PJT Partners, 6.4 times at Houlihan Lokey and 3.5 times at Lazard. On the screen's own metric, correctly computed, Moelis is the most expensive name in the group. The 9.8 times price to free cash flow is likewise a fiscal-2025 figure struck at a lower share price; on trailing cash flow at today's price it is 12.1 times.

Fifth, the cost base is now fixed and rising into a softening top line. Eight managing directors hired year-to-date in 2026 on top of 21 added in 2025, a new and larger London office, and continued technology and artificial-intelligence spend, with 2026 non-compensation expense guided to grow at a similar rate to 2025. Analysts have asked at every single call for a compensation-ratio formula or a flat-revenue sensitivity, and management has declined every time -- most pointedly in April 2026, when asked directly what happens to the ratio if revenue is flat: 'right now, we're not expecting that.' The honest reading is that a flat-revenue year would push the compensation ratio back up and compress margins hard, and nobody has been given the sensitivity.

Sixth, the five-year record undercuts the compounding narrative. Revenue: $1.54 billion in 2021, $985 million in 2022, $855 million in 2023, $1.19 billion in 2024, $1.52 billion in 2025. Earnings per share: $5.34, $2.14, a $0.36 loss, $1.78, $2.94. After a full cycle, revenue has merely returned to its 2021 level and earnings per share sit 45% below it -- a compound decline of roughly 14% a year. Book value per share has compounded at 0.1% a year, because virtually all earnings leave the company. This is a cyclical fee business that pays out what it earns, not a compounder.

Seventh, the dividend is thinly covered. The $0.65 quarterly payout is $2.60 a year against $2.78 of trailing earnings per share -- roughly 94%. Management calls it 'the first priority' and is committed to maintaining it, which in a downturn means funding it from a balance sheet that already fell from $849 million of cash and liquid investments at the end of 2025 to $354 million by 31 March 2026, and which carries $267 million of capitalised lease obligations against $153 million of cash.

Eighth, the market's own freshest opinion is bearish. UBS cut its target to $60 on 7 July 2026 with the stock at $69.84, arguing that expectations for advisory revenue and earnings were too optimistic and citing insider selling. Insiders have bought zero shares in the open market and sold 2,765. The only price targets above the market are stale -- Morgan Stanley's $83 dates to 9 April 2026 and the $82 to 20 January 2026.

What confirms the bear case: a second-quarter print on 29 July 2026 at or below the $0.64 consensus with no reacceleration in the second half, or any upward drift in the compensation ratio above 65.8%.

forcing_function:
There is no event on the calendar that forces a re-rating, and for a name trading above its base-case fair value that is the correct thing to say plainly.

The only hard date in the window is the second-quarter 2026 earnings report on 29 July 2026, confirmed by the company on 8 July 2026, with consensus at $0.64 of earnings per share on $387 million of revenue. That is a scheduled report rather than a structural event. It can move the price sharply -- last quarter's 15% miss shows how sharply -- but it settles one quarter, not the thesis, and it lands inside a crowded macro week (the Federal Reserve on 28 and 29 July, mega-cap technology capital-expenditure guidance on 29 and 30 July) that tends to mute single-name reactions.

The genuine forcing function for this thesis is not an event but a condition: the middle market opening. Management has promised it twice, in October 2025 and again in April 2026, with no date attached, and it depends on sponsor financing conditions the firm does not control. The observable that would confirm it is the mix of announced transaction sizes and a return to double-digit year-over-year revenue growth -- neither of which any calendar can schedule.

The secondary lever, the $300 million buyback authorised on 4 February 2026, has no expiry and no committed pace. At roughly 6% of the market value it is supportive but not transformative, and management has been explicit that its purpose is offsetting the dilution from stock compensation rather than shrinking the share count aggressively.

What is worth naming precisely, because it is what would change this rating: two consecutive quarters of double-digit revenue growth with the compensation ratio held at or below 65.8%, or a share price near $55 -- the base-case sum-of-the-parts value -- which would restore an actual margin of safety. Either would move this from pass to a live position. Neither is scheduled.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry no solvency risk whatsoever -- this firm has zero borrowed money, no maturity wall and no cash burn -- but they carry real multiple risk, and the first test is two days away.

The immediate hazard is the second-quarter report on 29 July 2026, with consensus at $0.64 of earnings per share on $387 million of revenue, roughly 6% year-over-year growth. Moelis missed by 15% last quarter, at $0.50 against $0.59. A second consecutive miss on a stock at 22 times forward earnings -- the highest multiple in the group -- would compress the multiple rather than the earnings. Worse, the print lands inside the densest event cluster of the year: the Federal Reserve meets 28 and 29 July, and the largest technology companies report capital-expenditure plans between 29 and 30 July. Company-specific news resolving inside that window tends to be drowned out, so a good print may be muted while a bad one still travels.

The second hazard is the driver management themselves named. On the 29 April 2026 call, 'disruptions in private credit' was listed among the headwinds -- and that disruption has since worsened rather than healed. The large private-credit vehicles began gating redemptions through early July 2026, with several enforcing withdrawal caps and one entering wind-down; sector default rates hit record levels. Private credit is the financing layer beneath sponsor-led buyouts, which are the demand source beneath Moelis's sponsor franchise, its private capital advisory build-out and much of its capital markets line. If sponsor financing stays tight through the autumn, the middle-market broadening that the whole bull case rests on gets pushed out for a third time.

The third hazard is the rate path, and it cuts against this thesis specifically. Policy is at 3.50% to 3.75% under a hawkish Federal Reserve, a December hike is the priced base case, and a hold is expected in July. Any version of this thesis that leans on cheaper financing to unlock deal volume is leaning on something the market is pricing in the opposite direction. Management deserves credit for not making that argument themselves -- asked directly about a Fed-driven selloff in October 2025, the chief executive said cost of money 'is a variable in transactional activity, but it's not the only variable' -- but the sponsor exit math does depend on it.

The fourth is a seasonal cash pattern that looks alarming and is not. Cash and liquid investments fell from $849 million at the end of 2025 to $354 million at 31 March 2026. That is the annual bonus payout plus $117 million of buybacks plus the dividend, and it recurs every first quarter. It is not deterioration. What it does mean is that the buffer funding a 94%-of-earnings dividend is thinner in the first half of any year than the headline balance sheet implies.

The fifth is the fixed-cost lag. The 2026 hiring class and the new London office are expensed now and earn later. If revenue is flat rather than up 11% as consensus assumes, the compensation ratio rises off 65.8% and the margin expansion story -- the single best-evidenced part of the bull case -- reverses in the very quarters investors are watching for confirmation.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical forced-selling dynamic here, and that is itself part of the problem -- there is no washout to wait for and no dislocated seller to buy from.

The shareholder base is stable and institutional. The company has no borrowed money, so there is no lender who can force anything. There is no pending transaction, index event, spin-off, lock-up expiry or strategic review to create price-insensitive flow. The stock sits 59% up its 52-week range, 2% above its 200-day average and near its 50-day, roughly 13% below the $78.22 high and well clear of the $51.06 low. The one shareholder cohort that could move mechanically is the income-oriented base. Moelis pays $0.65 quarterly, a 3.8% yield, which is high for the sector and is a genuine reason some holders own it. That dividend absorbs roughly 94% of trailing twelve-month diluted earnings of $2.78. moderator_conclusion:
This is a pass for now, and it is a pass on price rather than on quality.

Moelis & Company is a good firm and the recent operating record is genuinely strong. Full-year 2025 revenue grew 28% to $1.54 billion, the compensation ratio fell 320 basis points to 65.8%, pre-tax margin expanded 510 basis points to 21.5%, and adjusted earnings per share rose 64%. Management guided its most important cost line to the decimal and hit it. They called the April 2025 tariff shock correctly in public while it was happening. They flagged excess capital in July 2025 and were buying stock one quarter later. They executed a founder-to-successor handover without visible disruption. They built a seventh-and-eighth-banker private capital advisory team into a record sponsor-secondaries market while telling investors plainly it would not earn much in 2025. On the deep dive into management and the setup, this scores 4 out of 5 for credibility with a strengthening trajectory. None of that is in dispute.

The problem is arithmetic. Valuing the business by its parts -- mergers and acquisitions advisory at roughly $1,030 million of revenue on 3.0 times enterprise value to revenue, capital markets at $250 million on 2.5 times, capital structure advisory at $230 million on 2.5 times, private capital advisory at $30 million on 5.0 times, less $114 million of net debt across 79.5 million fully diluted shares -- produces about $55 a share. Two independent cross-checks agree: the peer-median trailing earnings multiple gives $54, the peer-median cash-earnings multiple gives $48, and applying the peer median to 2026 consensus earnings gives $60. The shares trade at $68.18, roughly 24% above that centre. There is no margin of safety; the market price already contains the favourable case.

Worse, the reason this name reached the committee at all is a measurement error. It was flagged as deep value on a screen using gross profit, but the data feed classifies banker compensation as cost of revenue in three quarters of four and omits it in the fourth, inflating trailing gross profit by roughly $295 million. Corrected, the metric that called this cheap makes it the most expensive name in its group -- about 10.8 times enterprise value to gross profit against 5.3 at PJT Partners, 6.4 at Houlihan Lokey and 3.5 at Lazard. Live peer multiples say the same thing on every other measure: Moelis at roughly 23 to 24.5 times trailing earnings against Evercore's 17.5, Lazard's 18.8, PJT Partners' 20.1 and Houlihan Lokey's 22.2. This is the peer group's highest multiple attached to the peer group's most recent earnings miss -- $0.50 against $0.59 on 29 April 2026, on 4% revenue growth after four quarters of 41%, 38%, 34% and 11%.

On timing, three things argue for patience rather than entry. The market regime is hostile to any thesis needing cheaper money: policy sits at 3.50% to 3.75% with a December hike the priced base case, so the sponsor-exit math that would open the middle market is not getting help from rates. The private-credit disruption management named as a headwind in April 2026 has worsened since, with major vehicles gating redemptions through early July -- and private credit is the financing layer beneath the sponsor franchise. And the second-quarter print on 29 July 2026 lands inside the year's densest macro week, where a good number gets muted and a bad one still travels.

One clarification on how this rating was set. A soft, non-binding catalyst is not a mark against a name in this book -- the dated-event names are handled elsewhere, and post-event re-rates frequently keep running. The absence of a hard catalyst here neither raised nor lowered the score. Both the overall rating and the standalone value rating come out at 2 for the same single reason: the price is roughly 24% above the base-case value of the parts, the adverse case is $42 and the favourable case is $87, and an investor buying today is paying for the favourable case while receiving the base one. On the value dimension judged in isolation, ignoring the catalyst question and the macro tilt entirely, the answer is the same -- this is a quality franchise with a narrow, relationship-based moat that is holding steady rather than widening, and no structural force threatens its long-term earnings power, but there is simply no discount to buy.

What would change this. A price near $55 restores a real margin of safety on a business we would be glad to own. Alternatively, two consecutive quarters of double-digit revenue growth with the compensation ratio held at or below 65.8% would validate that the 2025 operating leverage is a trend rather than a cyclical peak, and would justify revisiting the multiple. Until one of those arrives, this is a good business at the wrong price, surfaced by a screen that was measuring the wrong number.

# Moelis & Company (NYSE: MC) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator's deep dive on management and the setup. Five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (first quarter 2025 through first quarter 2026) cross-referenced against the reported financials. Prices and multiples are live as of 27 July 2026; the shares last traded at $68.18 on the New York Stock Exchange, in US dollars.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Moelis is an independent advisory firm — it earns fees for advising companies on mergers, acquisitions, capital raising and debt restructurings, and it holds almost no balance sheet risk of its own. Across these five calls the story moves through three distinct phases, and the movement is unusually easy to trace because management narrates it plainly.

**Phase one — shock and reassurance (first quarter 2025).** The call was held three weeks after the 2 April 2025 tariff announcement. Management had just posted 41% revenue growth and a record pipeline, and then watched the pipeline crack. Chief executive Ken Moelis was specific rather than evasive: "our backlog is down from $331 million as a result of it," and he separated the deals that were cancelled from the ones merely delayed — "the vast majority are in pushback." The framing was that the disruption was policy-made and therefore reversible: "it is in the control of the administration," unlike the global financial crisis or the pandemic. That is a testable claim, and it was later proved right.

**Phase two — validation and succession (second and third quarters 2025).** The recovery arrived faster than management had dared guide. By July 2025, "we're kind of back as of now very close to the level of enthusiasm that was prior to April 2." Revenue rose 38% in the second quarter and 34% in the third. Simultaneously the firm executed a founder-to-successor handover: Ken Moelis moved to executive chairman and co-founder Navid Mahmoodzadegan became chief executive, effective with the third-quarter call. The narrative also acquired a genuinely new growth leg — private capital advisory, which advises private-equity sponsors on continuation vehicles and secondary sales of fund stakes. Management called it a "fourth pillar" and staffed it deliberately, moving from a single hire to seven dedicated managing directors within twelve months.

**Phase three — record year, then a stall (fourth quarter 2025 and first quarter 2026).** The fourth quarter of 2025 was the high-water mark: record quarterly revenue of $488 million, full-year adjusted revenue of $1.54 billion (up 28%), and an adjusted pre-tax margin of 21.5%, up 5.1 percentage points from 2024. Then the first quarter of 2026 decelerated sharply — revenue of $320 million, up only 4% year over year, against year-over-year growth of 41%, 38%, 34% and 11% in the four preceding quarters. The language changed with it. For the first time in the sequence, management led with headwinds: "the war in the Middle East, disruptions in private credit and the impact of AI on certain sectors, have created some near-term headwinds in parts of the transactional environment."

**What was quietly dropped and what was added.** Capital markets — the standout of 2025, with revenue "more than double" the prior year through September — reversed to a year-over-year decline in the first quarter of 2026 and was mentioned far more briefly. Capital structure advisory (restructuring and liability management) has been in a two-year holding pattern: guided down for 2025 against a record 2024, then re-promoted in the first quarter of 2026 as a pipeline "meaningfully above last year's levels." The consistent new addition is private capital advisory, and it is the one line where the build-out is verifiable through headcount rather than rhetoric.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

The pipeline claim has been constant while the conversion rate has visibly slowed | **Diverges.** The pipeline may be full, but a claim repeated through a four-fold deceleration in growth has lost its information content |

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: rising through the third quarter of 2025, then flattening — currently stable with a defensive tilt.**

- *First quarter 2025 — defensive but specific.* "I don't think it's disastrous but it's not as good as I was hoping it was gonna be." Management quantified the damage rather than hiding it. High-quality defensiveness.
- *Second quarter 2025 — offensive.* "We entered the second half of the year in a significantly improved transaction environment." Specific, dated, and later validated.
- *Third quarter 2025 — most confident point in the file.* The new chief executive opened by name-checking three marquee mandates in a single week (Essential Utilities, the Delaware Attorney General on OpenAI's recapitalisation, the New York Giants) and asserted "a steadily improving multiyear M&A cycle." Confidence peaks here.
- *Fourth quarter 2025 — confident, and for once backed by the print.* "We closed 2025 with significant momentum."
- *First quarter 2026 — the tilt.* Headwinds are now named in the opening paragraph. The most revealing sentence is the concession on control: "we have to transact against that pipeline… some of that is out of our control." That is a materially different posture from a year earlier, when the constraint was framed as temporary and externally imposed.

**Guidance specificity has fallen deliberately.** In 2024 the firm gave analysts a compensation-ratio formula. That was withdrawn — "there's no formula. I think it's going to be driven by the top line" (second quarter 2025) — and by the first quarter of 2026 the chief financial officer declined again: "I don't think we're going to get into any sort of algorithm or percentages." Less specificity is not automatically evasion in a business with genuinely unforecastable revenue, but it does mean the firm has removed the one number analysts could have held it to.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: high.** This is the strongest part of the file, and it is why the deceleration in the first quarter of 2026 deserves to be read as a cycle event rather than a credibility event.

- *Non-compensation expense.* Guided to roughly 15% growth for 2025 in the first quarter of 2025, reiterated in the second and third quarters, and delivered — full-year non-compensation expense of $224 million, a 14.6% ratio, down from 15.9%. Then guided 2026 to "a similar rate," and the first quarter came in consistent with that. Four consecutive quarters of a guide made and kept.
- *The April 2025 disruption call.* Management said the shock was temporary and that most of the lost backlog was delayed rather than cancelled. Three months later revenue grew 38% and the pipeline was rebuilding. The judgement was right and it was made in public with the outcome unknown.
- *Excess capital.* Flagged in July 2025, acted on within one quarter, escalated in the fourth quarter, and formalised with a $300 million authorisation in February 2026.
- *The compensation ratio.* Guided to "a similar comp ratio to where we ended the year at… that 65.8%" for 2026 (fourth quarter 2025 call), and the first quarter of 2026 came in at exactly 65.8%.

**The earnings-beat record, and the crack in it.** Moelis beat consensus earnings in six of the last seven quarters — $0.22 versus $0.21, $1.18 versus $0.39, $0.64 versus $0.56, $0.53 versus $0.32, $0.68 versus $0.57, $1.13 versus $0.76 — and then **missed** on 29 April 2026, at $0.50 against $0.59. Two observations matter. First, the miss is the most recent data point, not an old one. Second, and less comfortably, at least one of the beats was manufactured below the revenue line: in the third quarter of 2025 revenue came in at $357 million on a reported basis against a $430 million estimate, yet earnings per share beat, because the compensation ratio was accrued down to 66.2%. Management controls the compensation accrual and uses it. That is legitimate and disclosed, but it means the beat rate measures expense discipline as much as it measures demand.

**Sandbagging pattern:** mild and structural. Fourth-quarter estimates are habitually far too low ($1.18 versus $0.39; $1.13 versus $0.76) because the annual compensation true-up lands in the fourth quarter and analysts consistently mis-model it. Read the beat rate accordingly.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The compensation ratio, asked at every single call, answered at none.** Ryan Kenny (Morgan Stanley) in the first and second quarters of 2025, Brendan O'Brien in the second, Ken Worthington (JPMorgan) in the fourth, Michael Brown in the first quarter of 2026 — all pressing for a formula, a threshold, or a sensitivity. The answers reduce to "it's all top-line driven." The unanswered question underneath is the one that matters for the equity: the firm has hired aggressively into private capital advisory and capital markets, those costs are fixed and already in the run-rate, and nobody has been told what happens to margins if revenue is flat. When Michael Brown asked exactly that in April 2026, the answer was "right now, we're not expecting that" — a non-answer to a scenario question.

**The middle market, asked repeatedly, still not arrived.** Analysts have asked since 2025 when activity broadens beyond large-cap deals. In October 2025: "we're definitely seeing the broadening… we think that's coming." In April 2026, six months later: "it will just take time for that middle market to open up, but it's coming." The same promise, re-dated. That is the clearest example in the file of a forecast that has been serially extended rather than delivered.

**Restructuring, promised counter-cyclically for two years.** Asked about restructuring in the first quarter of 2025, management said conversations were rising but mandates were not. By the third quarter of 2025 the business was in outright decline. By the first quarter of 2026 the pipeline was "meaningfully above last year's levels" and management expects "more traditional restructurings over time." The hedge that is supposed to work when mergers stall has, so far, declined at the same time mergers boomed and has not yet risen as mergers slowed.

**What analysts are not pressing on, and should be.** Nobody has asked why the dividend absorbs essentially all reported earnings. The $0.65 quarterly dividend is $2.60 a year against trailing twelve-month diluted earnings per share of $2.78 — a payout ratio near 94%. In a business that lost money as recently as 2023, that is a commitment management has called "the first priority… we're committed to maintaining," funded in a downturn from the balance sheet rather than from profits.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Growth deceleration, first quarter 2026.* From 41% to 4% year-over-year revenue growth in four quarters, with quarterly earnings per share down 25% year over year, and the first consensus miss in seven quarters.
- *A record label doing heavy lifting.* "Record first quarter revenues" (April 2026) describes a 4% growth quarter that missed by 15%. The gap between the adjective and the arithmetic opened for the first time in this sequence.
- *The pipeline claim has become non-falsifiable.* "Near record levels" has been asserted in four consecutive calls across a four-fold deceleration in conversion.
- *Fixed-cost build into a softening tape.* Managing director count rose from 170 (September 2025) to 178 (February 2026) with eight more hired year-to-date in 2026, plus a new, larger London office. These costs land whether or not the middle market opens.
- *Insider behaviour.* Zero open-market purchases against one open-market sale (2,765 shares). Small in size, but there is no insider vote of confidence at this price, and UBS explicitly cited insider selling when it cut its target to $60 on 7 July 2026 with the stock at $69.84.
- *The dividend consumes almost all earnings.* Roughly 94% of trailing earnings per share, in a cyclical business that has printed a loss inside the last three years.
- *Capital markets reversed.* The 2025 star — revenue more than doubling through September — turned to a year-over-year decline in the first quarter of 2026, and the initial-public-offering window has cooled since.

**Green flags**

- *The operating leverage is real and audited.* Compensation ratio 69% to 65.8%; non-compensation ratio 15.9% to 14.6%; adjusted pre-tax margin 16.4% to 21.5%; adjusted earnings per share up 64% in 2025. This is the best evidence in the file that the 2023-2024 hiring has paid.
- *Capital returned promptly and at sensible prices.* Buybacks at averages of $62.96 (fourth quarter 2025) and $61.40 (first quarter 2026) — below today's $68 — plus a $300 million authorisation. Management bought when the stock was cheaper than it is now, which is both a green flag on discipline and a caution on the current price.
- *A succession executed without disruption.* Founder to co-founder, announced in July 2025, effective October 2025, with no visible change in tone, strategy or senior attrition.
- *Candour under pressure.* Quantifying the lost backlog in April 2025, and stating plainly that private capital advisory would not generate meaningful 2025 revenue, are both instances of management declining an easy spin.
- *A genuine new revenue leg being built the hard way.* Seven managing directors dedicated to sponsor-led secondaries, hired into a market that is at record volumes, and plugged into pre-existing sponsor relationships — the fastest-ramping form of advisory hire, as management explained in July 2025.
- *No borrowed money.* Whatever the lease accounting says, the firm has zero funded debt and cannot be forced by a lender in a downturn.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary of control changed.** In April 2025 the constraint was external and temporary — "it is in the control of the administration." In April 2026 the constraint moved inside the sentence: "we have to transact against that pipeline… some of that is out of our control." Management stopped promising the conversion and started describing it as a variable.

**"Record" became load-bearing.** The word appears in every call, but its function shifts. In 2025 it described results that also grew 28-41%. In April 2026 it described a 4% growth quarter that missed consensus. When a superlative has to carry a soft number, it is being used to manage the frame.

**Competition was reframed from banks to boutiques.** Asked in February 2026 whether deregulation had re-armed the large universal banks, the answer redirected: "a lot of the times, we're competing against independent firms like us." That is a quiet acknowledgement that the pressure comes from firms with the same model, the same economics and the same ability to pay for talent — which is exactly why the compensation ratio is the number that decides this equity.

**Artificial intelligence is discussed as an opportunity in three separate directions and as a threat in none.** It is a source of restructuring mandates (companies disrupted by it), a source of capital-markets mandates (companies building it), and an internal productivity lever ("a clear productivity lever supporting our bankers"). That reading looks right for board-level advisory work, which is bought on relationships and judgement rather than on document output, but it is worth noting that management has not been pressed on it once.

**The new chief executive is more structured and slightly more promotional.** Navid Mahmoodzadegan organises calls by product pillar and names marquee mandates; Ken Moelis spoke in improvised analogies and volunteered bad news faster. Neither is worse, but the disclosure texture has shifted from confessional to curated.

**The methodology flag that surfaced this name is an accounting artifact — the most important hidden signal here.** This company reached the committee through a screen on enterprise value to gross profit, showing gross margin at 99.2% and a price to free cash flow of 9.8 times. Neither figure survives inspection. The 99.2% gross margin comes from the fourth quarter of 2025, where the data feed classified almost no compensation as cost of revenue, while the other three quarters classify roughly two-thirds of revenue that way — inflating trailing gross profit by close to $295 million. Restating the fourth quarter consistently (at the disclosed 61.1% compensation ratio), trailing gross profit is roughly $514 million, not $809 million, and enterprise value to gross profit is about 10.8 times rather than the 6.8 times the raw feed implies — against roughly 5.3 times at PJT Partners, 6.4 times at Houlihan Lokey and 3.5 times at Lazard. Likewise the 9.8 times price to free cash flow is a fiscal-2025 figure struck at a lower share price; on trailing twelve-month cash flow at today's price it is 12.1 times. **On the screen's own metric, correctly computed, Moelis is the most expensive name in its peer group, not the cheapest.** The "deep value" label attached to this candidate does not survive the arithmetic.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory classification: strengthening — but the strengthening is a cyclical recovery to a prior peak, and the most recent quarter broke the sequence.**

The operating evidence is good and it is corroborated: 28% revenue growth in 2025, 510 basis points of pre-tax margin improvement, a compensation ratio guided and hit to the decimal, a founder succession executed cleanly, capital returned promptly and at prices below today's, zero borrowed money, and a credible new business line staffed with seven senior people into a record secondaries market. Management's forecasting record over these five calls is genuinely high quality — they called the April 2025 shock correctly, kept every expense guide, and delivered the capital return they signalled.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position is that none of the above is a valuation argument, and the valuation is where this name fails.** At $68.18 the shares trade at roughly 24.5 times trailing diluted earnings, 22 times the 2026 consensus of $3.09, about 17.2 times trailing enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, and 3.6 times enterprise value to revenue. Every one of those is the highest in the peer group as measured live today: Evercore at 17.5 times trailing earnings and 12.4 times enterprise value to that cash-earnings measure, PJT Partners at 20.1 and 11.0, Houlihan Lokey at 22.2 and 13.9, Lazard at 18.8 and 13.2. The premium is being paid for a firm whose most recent quarter grew 4% and missed, whose newest analyst target ($60, UBS, 7 July 2026) sits 12% below the market price, and whose five-year earnings-per-share trend is negative. The director is not choosing whether this is a good business — it is — but whether to pay the group's highest multiple for the group's most recently disappointing quarter.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is intangible brand plus relationships — the Moelis name, the sponsor coverage franchise, and 178 managing directors whose client relationships are the actual asset. It is real: the firm has demonstrably taken share, its capital-markets and technology teams have "been a stunning success" on management's own account, and clients pay for judgement in situations where being wrong is expensive. But it is narrow, for three structural reasons. There are no switching costs — every mandate is re-won. The asset walks: management describes talent acquisition as "hand-to-hand combat" and identifies its main competitors as firms with an identical model. And the returns evidence, while high, is earned on almost no capital, so a 21.7% return on invested capital describes an asset-light fee model rather than a defended franchise. On width and direction, the returns are improving, not eroding — margins expanded 510 basis points in 2025 and headcount is growing — so the honest reading is a narrow moat holding steady, not one being structurally cut away.

**Secular threat to terminal value: manageable.** Board-level advice on a $6 billion sale is bought on trust, discretion and accountability, not on document production; generative artificial intelligence attacks the input cost of junior banking work, which flows to Moelis as a margin tailwind, and management is deploying it as such. The two genuine structural risks are different in kind and both are cyclical-to-competitive rather than terminal: fee compression from an over-supplied independent-advisory sector all hiring the same people, and the fact that the entire revenue line depends on a merger cycle the firm does not control. There is no structural force here that shrinks the addressable market — global merger activity set an all-time first-half record of about $2.8 trillion in 2026. **The cheapness is not a fear-print, because there is no cheapness: the multiple is a premium and the risk is that a high-quality cyclical is being priced at the wrong point in its own cycle.**

Moelis & Company is a good firm and the recent operating record is genuinely strong. The market regime is hostile to any thesis needing cheaper money: policy sits at 3.50% to 3.75% with a December hike the priced base case, so the sponsor-exit math that would open the middle market is not getting help from rates. A soft, non-binding catalyst is not a mark against a name in this book -- the dated-event names are handled elsewhere, and post-event re-rates frequently keep running. The absence of a hard catalyst here neither raised nor lowered the score. # Moelis & Company (NYSE: MC) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator's deep dive on management and the setup. Five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (first quarter 2025 through first quarter 2026) cross-referenced against the reported financials. Prices and multiples are live as of 27 July 2026; the shares last traded at $68.18 on the New York Stock Exchange, in US dollars.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Moelis is an independent advisory firm — it earns fees for advising companies on mergers, acquisitions, capital raising and debt restructurings, and it holds almost no balance sheet risk of its own. Across these five calls the story moves through three distinct phases, and the movement is unusually easy to trace because management narrates it plainly.

**Phase one — shock and reassurance (first quarter 2025).** The call was held three weeks after the 2 April 2025 tariff announcement. Management had just posted 41% revenue growth and a record pipeline, and then watched the pipeline crack. Chief executive Ken Moelis was specific rather than evasive: "our backlog is down from $331 million as a result of it," and he separated the deals that were cancelled from the ones merely delayed — "the vast majority are in pushback." The framing was that the disruption was policy-made and therefore reversible: "it is in the control of the administration," unlike the global financial crisis or the pandemic. That is a testable claim, and it was later proved right.

**Phase two — validation and succession (second and third quarters 2025).** The recovery arrived faster than management had dared guide. By July 2025, "we're kind of back as of now very close to the level of enthusiasm that was prior to April 2." Revenue rose 38% in the second quarter and 34% in the third. Simultaneously the firm executed a founder-to-successor handover: Ken Moelis moved to executive chairman and co-founder Navid Mahmoodzadegan became chief executive, effective with the third-quarter call. The narrative also acquired a genuinely new growth leg — private capital advisory, which advises private-equity sponsors on continuation vehicles and secondary sales of fund stakes. Management called it a "fourth pillar" and staffed it deliberately, moving from a single hire to seven dedicated managing directors within twelve months.

**Phase three — record year, then a stall (fourth quarter 2025 and first quarter 2026).** The fourth quarter of 2025 was the high-water mark: record quarterly revenue of $488 million, full-year adjusted revenue of $1.54 billion (up 28%), and an adjusted pre-tax margin of 21.5%, up 5.1 percentage points from 2024. Then the first quarter of 2026 decelerated sharply — revenue of $320 million, up only 4% year over year, against year-over-year growth of 41%, 38%, 34% and 11% in the four preceding quarters. The language changed with it. For the first time in the sequence, management led with headwinds: "the war in the Middle East, disruptions in private credit and the impact of AI on certain sectors, have created some near-term headwinds in parts of the transactional environment."

**What was quietly dropped and what was added.** Capital markets — the standout of 2025, with revenue "more than double" the prior year through September — reversed to a year-over-year decline in the first quarter of 2026 and was mentioned far more briefly. Capital structure advisory (restructuring and liability management) has been in a two-year holding pattern: guided down for 2025 against a record 2024, then re-promoted in the first quarter of 2026 as a pipeline "meaningfully above last year's levels." The consistent new addition is private capital advisory, and it is the one line where the build-out is verifiable through headcount rather than rhetoric.

- *Fourth quarter 2025 — confident, and for once backed by the print.* "We closed 2025 with significant momentum."
- *First quarter 2026 — the tilt.* Headwinds are now named in the opening paragraph. The most revealing sentence is the concession on control: "we have to transact against that pipeline… some of that is out of our control." That is a materially different posture from a year earlier, when the constraint was framed as temporary and externally imposed.

**Guidance specificity has fallen deliberately.** In 2024 the firm gave analysts a compensation-ratio formula. That was withdrawn — "there's no formula. I think it's going to be driven by the top line" (second quarter 2025) — and by the first quarter of 2026 the chief financial officer declined again: "I don't think we're going to get into any sort of algorithm or percentages." Less specificity is not automatically evasion in a business with genuinely unforecastable revenue, but it does mean the firm has removed the one number analysts could have held it to.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: high.** This is the strongest part of the file, and it is why the deceleration in the first quarter of 2026 deserves to be read as a cycle event rather than a credibility event.

- *Non-compensation expense.* Guided to roughly 15% growth for 2025 in the first quarter of 2025, reiterated in the second and third quarters, and delivered — full-year non-compensation expense of $224 million, a 14.6% ratio, down from 15.9%. Then guided 2026 to "a similar rate," and the first quarter came in consistent with that. Four consecutive quarters of a guide made and kept.
- *The April 2025 disruption call.* Management said the shock was temporary and that most of the lost backlog was delayed rather than cancelled. Three months later revenue grew 38% and the pipeline was rebuilding. The judgement was right and it was made in public with the outcome unknown.
- *Excess capital.* Flagged in July 2025, acted on within one quarter, escalated in the fourth quarter, and formalised with a $300 million authorisation in February 2026.
- *The compensation ratio.* Guided to "a similar comp ratio to where we ended the year at… that 65.8%" for 2026 (fourth quarter 2025 call), and the first quarter of 2026 came in at exactly 65.8%.

**The earnings-beat record, and the crack in it.** Moelis beat consensus earnings in six of the last seven quarters — $0.22 versus $0.21, $1.18 versus $0.39, $0.64 versus $0.56, $0.53 versus $0.32, $0.68 versus $0.57, $1.13 versus $0.76 — and then **missed** on 29 April 2026, at $0.50 against $0.59. Two observations matter. First, the miss is the most recent data point, not an old one. Second, and less comfortably, at least one of the beats was manufactured below the revenue line: in the third quarter of 2025 revenue came in at $357 million on a reported basis against a $430 million estimate, yet earnings per share beat, because the compensation ratio was accrued down to 66.2%. Management controls the compensation accrual and uses it. That is legitimate and disclosed, but it means the beat rate measures expense discipline as much as it measures demand.

**Sandbagging pattern:** mild and structural. Fourth-quarter estimates are habitually far too low ($1.18 versus $0.39; $1.13 versus $0.76) because the annual compensation true-up lands in the fourth quarter and analysts consistently mis-model it. Read the beat rate accordingly.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The compensation ratio, asked at every single call, answered at none.** Ryan Kenny (Morgan Stanley) in the first and second quarters of 2025, Brendan O'Brien in the second, Ken Worthington (JPMorgan) in the fourth, Michael Brown in the first quarter of 2026 — all pressing for a formula, a threshold, or a sensitivity. The answers reduce to "it's all top-line driven." The unanswered question underneath is the one that matters for the equity: the firm has hired aggressively into private capital advisory and capital markets, those costs are fixed and already in the run-rate, and nobody has been told what happens to margins if revenue is flat. When Michael Brown asked exactly that in April 2026, the answer was "right now, we're not expecting that" — a non-answer to a scenario question.

**The middle market, asked repeatedly, still not arrived.** Analysts have asked since 2025 when activity broadens beyond large-cap deals. In October 2025: "we're definitely seeing the broadening… we think that's coming." In April 2026, six months later: "it will just take time for that middle market to open up, but it's coming." The same promise, re-dated. That is the clearest example in the file of a forecast that has been serially extended rather than delivered.

**Restructuring, promised counter-cyclically for two years.** Asked about restructuring in the first quarter of 2025, management said conversations were rising but mandates were not. By the third quarter of 2025 the business was in outright decline. By the first quarter of 2026 the pipeline was "meaningfully above last year's levels" and management expects "more traditional restructurings over time." The hedge that is supposed to work when mergers stall has, so far, declined at the same time mergers boomed and has not yet risen as mergers slowed.

**What analysts are not pressing on, and should be.** Nobody has asked why the dividend absorbs essentially all reported earnings. The $0.65 quarterly dividend is $2.60 a year against trailing twelve-month diluted earnings per share of $2.78 — a payout ratio near 94%. In a business that lost money as recently as 2023, that is a commitment management has called "the first priority… we're committed to maintaining," funded in a downturn from the balance sheet rather than from profits.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Growth deceleration, first quarter 2026.* From 41% to 4% year-over-year revenue growth in four quarters, with quarterly earnings per share down 25% year over year, and the first consensus miss in seven quarters.
- *A record label doing heavy lifting.* "Record first quarter revenues" (April 2026) describes a 4% growth quarter that missed by 15%. The gap between the adjective and the arithmetic opened for the first time in this sequence.
- *The pipeline claim has become non-falsifiable.* "Near record levels" has been asserted in four consecutive calls across a four-fold deceleration in conversion.
- *Fixed-cost build into a softening tape.* Managing director count rose from 170 (September 2025) to 178 (February 2026) with eight more hired year-to-date in 2026, plus a new, larger London office. These costs land whether or not the middle market opens.
- *Insider behaviour.* Zero open-market purchases against one open-market sale (2,765 shares). Small in size, but there is no insider vote of confidence at this price, and UBS explicitly cited insider selling when it cut its target to $60 on 7 July 2026 with the stock at $69.84.
- *The dividend consumes almost all earnings.* Roughly 94% of trailing earnings per share, in a cyclical business that has printed a loss inside the last three years.
- *Capital markets reversed.* The 2025 star — revenue more than doubling through September — turned to a year-over-year decline in the first quarter of 2026, and the initial-public-offering window has cooled since.

**Green flags**

- *The operating leverage is real and audited.* Compensation ratio 69% to 65.8%; non-compensation ratio 15.9% to 14.6%; adjusted pre-tax margin 16.4% to 21.5%; adjusted earnings per share up 64% in 2025. This is the best evidence in the file that the 2023-2024 hiring has paid.
- *Capital returned promptly and at sensible prices.* Buybacks at averages of $62.96 (fourth quarter 2025) and $61.40 (first quarter 2026) — below today's $68 — plus a $300 million authorisation. Management bought when the stock was cheaper than it is now, which is both a green flag on discipline and a caution on the current price.
- *A succession executed without disruption.* Founder to co-founder, announced in July 2025, effective October 2025, with no visible change in tone, strategy or senior attrition.
- *Candour under pressure.* Quantifying the lost backlog in April 2025, and stating plainly that private capital advisory would not generate meaningful 2025 revenue, are both instances of management declining an easy spin.
- *A genuine new revenue leg being built the hard way.* Seven managing directors dedicated to sponsor-led secondaries, hired into a market that is at record volumes, and plugged into pre-existing sponsor relationships — the fastest-ramping form of advisory hire, as management explained in July 2025.
- *No borrowed money.* Whatever the lease accounting says, the firm has zero funded debt and cannot be forced by a lender in a downturn.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary of control changed.** In April 2025 the constraint was external and temporary — "it is in the control of the administration." In April 2026 the constraint moved inside the sentence: "we have to transact against that pipeline… some of that is out of our control." Management stopped promising the conversion and started describing it as a variable.

**"Record" became load-bearing.** The word appears in every call, but its function shifts. In 2025 it described results that also grew 28-41%. In April 2026 it described a 4% growth quarter that missed consensus. When a superlative has to carry a soft number, it is being used to manage the frame.

**Competition was reframed from banks to boutiques.** Asked in February 2026 whether deregulation had re-armed the large universal banks, the answer redirected: "a lot of the times, we're competing against independent firms like us." That is a quiet acknowledgement that the pressure comes from firms with the same model, the same economics and the same ability to pay for talent — which is exactly why the compensation ratio is the number that decides this equity.

**Artificial intelligence is discussed as an opportunity in three separate directions and as a threat in none.** It is a source of restructuring mandates (companies disrupted by it), a source of capital-markets mandates (companies building it), and an internal productivity lever ("a clear productivity lever supporting our bankers"). That reading looks right for board-level advisory work, which is bought on relationships and judgement rather than on document output, but it is worth noting that management has not been pressed on it once.

**The new chief executive is more structured and slightly more promotional.** Navid Mahmoodzadegan organises calls by product pillar and names marquee mandates; Ken Moelis spoke in improvised analogies and volunteered bad news faster. Neither is worse, but the disclosure texture has shifted from confessional to curated.

**The methodology flag that surfaced this name is an accounting artifact — the most important hidden signal here.** This company reached the committee through a screen on enterprise value to gross profit, showing gross margin at 99.2% and a price to free cash flow of 9.8 times. Neither figure survives inspection. The 99.2% gross margin comes from the fourth quarter of 2025, where the data feed classified almost no compensation as cost of revenue, while the other three quarters classify roughly two-thirds of revenue that way — inflating trailing gross profit by close to $295 million. Restating the fourth quarter consistently (at the disclosed 61.1% compensation ratio), trailing gross profit is roughly $514 million, not $809 million, and enterprise value to gross profit is about 10.8 times rather than the 6.8 times the raw feed implies — against roughly 5.3 times at PJT Partners, 6.4 times at Houlihan Lokey and 3.5 times at Lazard. Likewise the 9.8 times price to free cash flow is a fiscal-2025 figure struck at a lower share price; on trailing twelve-month cash flow at today's price it is 12.1 times. **On the screen's own metric, correctly computed, Moelis is the most expensive name in its peer group, not the cheapest.** The "deep value" label attached to this candidate does not survive the arithmetic.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory classification: strengthening — but the strengthening is a cyclical recovery to a prior peak, and the most recent quarter broke the sequence.**

The operating evidence is good and it is corroborated: 28% revenue growth in 2025, 510 basis points of pre-tax margin improvement, a compensation ratio guided and hit to the decimal, a founder succession executed cleanly, capital returned promptly and at prices below today's, zero borrowed money, and a credible new business line staffed with seven senior people into a record secondaries market. Management's forecasting record over these five calls is genuinely high quality — they called the April 2025 shock correctly, kept every expense guide, and delivered the capital return they signalled.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position is that none of the above is a valuation argument, and the valuation is where this name fails.** At $68.18 the shares trade at roughly 24.5 times trailing diluted earnings, 22 times the 2026 consensus of $3.09, about 17.2 times trailing enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, and 3.6 times enterprise value to revenue. Every one of those is the highest in the peer group as measured live today: Evercore at 17.5 times trailing earnings and 12.4 times enterprise value to that cash-earnings measure, PJT Partners at 20.1 and 11.0, Houlihan Lokey at 22.2 and 13.9, Lazard at 18.8 and 13.2. The premium is being paid for a firm whose most recent quarter grew 4% and missed, whose newest analyst target ($60, UBS, 7 July 2026) sits 12% below the market price, and whose five-year earnings-per-share trend is negative. The director is not choosing whether this is a good business — it is — but whether to pay the group's highest multiple for the group's most recently disappointing quarter.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is intangible brand plus relationships — the Moelis name, the sponsor coverage franchise, and 178 managing directors whose client relationships are the actual asset. It is real: the firm has demonstrably taken share, its capital-markets and technology teams have "been a stunning success" on management's own account, and clients pay for judgement in situations where being wrong is expensive. But it is narrow, for three structural reasons. There are no switching costs — every mandate is re-won. The asset walks: management describes talent acquisition as "hand-to-hand combat" and identifies its main competitors as firms with an identical model. And the returns evidence, while high, is earned on almost no capital, so a 21.7% return on invested capital describes an asset-light fee model rather than a defended franchise. On width and direction, the returns are improving, not eroding — margins expanded 510 basis points in 2025 and headcount is growing — so the honest reading is a narrow moat holding steady, not one being structurally cut away.

**Secular threat to terminal value: manageable.** Board-level advice on a $6 billion sale is bought on trust, discretion and accountability, not on document production; generative artificial intelligence attacks the input cost of junior banking work, which flows to Moelis as a margin tailwind, and management is deploying it as such. The two genuine structural risks are different in kind and both are cyclical-to-competitive rather than terminal: fee compression from an over-supplied independent-advisory sector all hiring the same people, and the fact that the entire revenue line depends on a merger cycle the firm does not control. There is no structural force here that shrinks the addressable market — global merger activity set an all-time first-half record of about $2.8 trillion in 2026. **The cheapness is not a fear-print, because there is no cheapness: the multiple is a premium and the risk is that a high-quality cyclical is being priced at the wrong point in its own cycle.**
